slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Vaginal discharge (swab; slides with saline and 10% KOH)

What it is used for: Done to find the cause of vaginal discharge, itching, burning or odour. The infections most often responsible are bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis and vulvovaginal candidiasis; cervicitis can also cause discharge. CDC notes that history alone is not enough for an accurate diagnosis, so examination and laboratory testing are needed.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Method: vaginal pH is measured with pH paper (pH > 4.5 is common with BV or trichomoniasis, though trichomoniasis can occur at normal pH). One sample is diluted in 1–2 drops of 0.9% saline and a second in 10% KOH; an amine (fishy) odour right after adding KOH suggests BV or trichomoniasis. With coverslips in place, slides are examined at low and high power: the saline slide may show motile trichomonads or clue cells (epithelial cells whose borders are obscured by small bacteria); the KOH slide shows hyphae or blastospores of candidiasis.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: Positive result: BV is diagnosed by the Amsel criteria — at least three of four: homogeneous thin (milk-like) discharge smoothly coating the vaginal walls; clue cells on microscopy; vaginal fluid pH > 4.5; a fishy odour before or after adding 10% KOH (whiff test). The laboratory reference standard is the Nugent score on a Gram-stained smear: 0–3 Lactobacillus-predominant, 4–6 intermediate, 7–10 BV.

Positive result: Motile trichomonads mean trichomoniasis; the provider prescribes treatment, partners should be tested, and testing for other STIs is advised. Many white cells without trichomonads or yeast may indicate cervicitis.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Negative result: Absence of trichomonads in saline or fungal elements in KOH does not rule out these infections: microscopy is about 50% sensitive compared with NAAT (trichomoniasis) or culture (yeast). For trichomoniasis the wet mount is 44–68% sensitive, so a negative wet mount should be followed by a molecular test when possible.

slides.title: Vaginal wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample is taken from vaginal discharge with a cotton swab or stick during a speculum exam. Usually tampons, vaginal creams or medicines and vaginal sex are avoided for 24 hours before. Read the slide immediately: wet-mount sensitivity for trichomonads drops to 20% within one hour of collection.

Per the official source, avoid tampons, vaginal creams and medicines, and vaginal sex for 24 hours before sampling. The textbook is stricter: no swab during a period or for 1–2 days after it, and vaginal suppositories and tablets stopped 2–3 days before — follow your laboratory’s instructions.

Limitations: A pH test alone cannot diagnose BV (healthy vaginal pH is 3.8–4.5). Pap tests are of no use for BV, and culture of Gardnerella vaginalis is not recommended because it is not specific. BV NAATs are for symptomatic women only.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Cervical cells collected with a brush or spatula (smear or liquid-based vial)

What it is used for: The Pap test screens for cervical cancer: it aims to find precancerous changes before symptoms appear, so treatment can prevent cancer. It also helps find cancer early, when it is easier to treat, and sometimes shows infection or inflammation.

US recommendations (as summarised by NCI): USPSTF — Pap test every 3 years at ages 21–29; at 30–65, an HPV test every 5 years, an HPV/Pap cotest every 5 years, or a Pap test every 3 years. ACS — an HPV test every 5 years from 25 to 65 (cotest every 5 years or Pap every 3 years remain acceptable). After 65, with regular normal results, screening is usually no longer needed. HIV, a weakened immune system or a recent abnormal result may call for more frequent screening.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Cervical cancer develops slowly: first, abnormal changes called dysplasia appear in the cells; if not removed, they may become cancer over time. Long-lasting infection with high-risk HPV types causes almost all cervical cancers.
Besides the conventional smear there is liquid-based cytology (for example ThinPrep); one advantage is that HPV testing can be done on the same preparation, one disadvantage is higher cost.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: Cytology and histology terms correspond: LSIL on a Pap test is generally CIN 1 on biopsy, and HSIL can be CIN 2, CIN 2/3 or CIN 3. CIN 1 often goes away on its own; CIN 3 is not cancer but may become cancer if untreated.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: An abnormal result does not mean cancer. For ASC-US an HPV test is usually done. Next steps follow ASCCP risk-based guidelines, weighing current and past results, prior treatment and age: a repeat test in 1 or 3 years, colposcopy with biopsy, or treatment.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: For 2 days before the test, avoid vaginal sex, douching, vaginal medicines and spermicidal foam or cream; MedlinePlus also advises avoiding tampons. Sources differ on periods: MedlinePlus advises not testing during your period (about 5 days after it ends is a good time), while CDC says both tests can still be done during a period — follow your provider's or laboratory's instructions.

Limitations: A single Pap test detects high-grade lesions with a sensitivity of 55–80%; a programme of regular testing is likely more sensitive. False positives can lead to unnecessary follow-up and procedures, and false negatives can delay care.

A Pap test does not diagnose cancer — colposcopy and biopsy do. Pap tests have no use for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis; trichomonads may be seen incidentally on a Pap smear, but that is not diagnostic and should be confirmed with a sensitive test.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Cervical cells (clinician-collected) or a self-collected vaginal swab

What it is used for: The HPV test looks in a sample of cervical cells for the infection that causes precancer and cancer. It is done alone (primary screening), with a Pap test (cotesting), or after an abnormal Pap — for example, ASC-US, to see whether HPV caused the changes. The screening schedule is on the Pap test card.

Physiology: HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses: low-risk types cause warts, while high-risk types can cause cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar, vaginal and penile cancers. The test detects DNA or RNA from high-risk HPV. HPV usually spreads through sexual contact, is especially common at ages 21–29, and usually clears on its own within a year or two.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: A positive result means high-risk HPV was found. It does not mean you have or will get precancer or cancer, but it raises future risk. There is no treatment for the HPV infection itself; next steps (colposcopy, more frequent testing) depend on past results, age and other factors.

Positive result: A positive test after several negative ones is not necessarily a new infection: HPV can become active again after many years. Whether a reactivated infection carries the same risk as a new one is not known.
Negative result: A negative result means high-risk HPV was not found. Per NCI, the next test is in 5 years; you may need to return sooner if you had abnormal results in the past.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample is taken by the provider from the cervix with a speculum and soft brush, or self-collected in a clinic by inserting and rotating a swab in the vagina. An HPV test alone needs no preparation. For 2 days before a cotest, avoid vaginal sex, douching, vaginal medicines and spermicides; tell the provider about recent sex or a period.

A Pap smear (cotest) is not done during a period — about 5 days after it ends is a good time; for 2 days before, avoid tampons, vaginal creams and medicines, douching and vaginal sex. An HPV test alone needs no preparation; tell the provider if you have your period. The textbook advises stopping vaginal suppositories 2–3 days before.
Limitations: HPV vaccination does not prevent infection with all high-risk types, so vaccinated people should still be screened.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Self-collected HPV testing may improve access to screening; in a pooled analysis of studies in China, however, self-collected samples were less sensitive for CIN 2+ (about 86%) than physician-collected samples (about 97%).

slides.title: Superficial squamous cell
slides.caption:
1 — Broad, flat, polygonal cytoplasm.
2 — Small, dense (pyknotic) nucleus.
What it looks like: Large, thin, polygonal cell. Pink-orange (eosinophilic) cytoplasm. Very small, dark, dense — pyknotic — nucleus.
Key feature: Tiny dot-like dark nucleus + pink cytoplasm.
What it means: The most mature epithelial layer. Present in a normal smear; predominance reflects oestrogen effect.
Confused with: Intermediate cell — larger vesicular nucleus, bluish cytoplasm.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: Often pink, but staining colour varies.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Intermediate squamous cell
slides.caption:
1 — Broad, usually blue-green cytoplasm.
2 — Vesicular nucleus, larger than in a superficial cell.
What it looks like: Large polygonal cell, edges often folded. Blue-green (cyanophilic) cytoplasm. Medium vesicular nucleus with fine chromatin.
Key feature: Its nucleus is the "ruler" other nuclei are compared with.
What it means: The main cell of a normal smear.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: A handy nuclear reference; size varies with preparation and condition.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Parabasal cell
slides.caption:
1 — Smaller round or oval cells with dense cytoplasm.
2 — Larger nuclear share than intermediate and superficial cells.
What it looks like: Smaller, round or oval. Dense blue-green cytoplasm. Relatively large nucleus.
Key feature: Round shape and dense cytoplasm.
What it means: Deep epithelial layer. Many of them suggest low oestrogen (menopause, postpartum) — an atrophic smear.
Confused with: Metaplastic cell, HSIL cell — look at the nucleus.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: A parabasal cell with a regular nucleus is not HSIL.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Endocervical (columnar) cells
slides.caption:
1 — En face: an orderly honeycomb sheet.
2 — Side view: columnar cells with basal nuclei.
What it looks like: En face — a "honeycomb" sheet. Side view — tall cells with basal nuclei in a row ("picket fence").
Key feature: Honeycomb or picket fence.
What it means: From the endocervical canal. Their presence shows the transformation zone was sampled (specimen adequacy).
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: Two views of the same epithelium; not all cells are ciliated.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Squamous metaplastic cell
slides.caption:
1 — Dense cytoplasm; round or oval, usually regular nucleus.
2 — Some cells show an angular outline or cytoplasmic process.
What it looks like: Medium size, dense blue-green cytoplasm, often with processes ("spider" cell). Oval, smooth nucleus.
Key feature: Cytoplasmic processes.
What it means: From the transformation zone; a normal finding.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: Not identified by processes alone; appearance changes with maturation.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Lactobacilli (Döderlein bacilli)
slides.caption:
1 — Long rods staining purple on Gram.
2 — An epithelial cell for comparison.
What it looks like: Long thin rods, abundant in the background and on cells.
Key feature: Many long rods, few cocci.
What it means: Normal vaginal flora; keeps the environment acidic. When abundant, intermediate cells may be lysed (cytolysis).
Stain / preparation: Gram; also visible on Pap
Caveat: Rod shape does not identify the species; there is no single "normal count".
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Clue cell
slides.caption:
1 — Small bacteria densely adhering to the cell surface.
2 — Bacteria blur the cell border as well.
What it looks like: A squamous cell covered with small coccobacilli; shaggy, indistinct borders. Few lactobacilli in the background.
Key feature: The cell border is obscured by bacteria.
What it means: A sign of bacterial vaginosis (one of Amsel’s criteria). The clinician diagnoses on the full set of criteria.
Confused with: An ordinary cell with a few bacteria — if the edges are still sharp, it is not a clue cell.
Stain / preparation: Wet mount / Gram / Pap
Caveat: One sign of bacterial vaginosis; never a diagnosis on its own.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Trichomonas vaginalis
slides.caption:
1 — Pear-shaped body; nucleus in the broad anterior part.
2 — Four anterior flagella; recurrent flagellum, undulating membrane and axostyle.
What it looks like: Pear-shaped grey-green body with a pale, elongated, eccentric nucleus and red cytoplasmic granules. Flagella are often not seen in stained smears.
Key feature: Pear shape + pale eccentric nucleus. Motile in a wet mount.
What it means: Trichomoniasis, usually with many neutrophils. A sensitive test (NAAT) is recommended to confirm.
Confused with: Cell fragments, degenerated leukocytes.
Stain / preparation: Wet mount or stained smear
Caveat: A structural diagram. Wet mounts show motility; flagella may not be visible on Pap. A negative wet mount does not exclude infection.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Candida (yeast)
slides.caption:
1 — Budding oval yeast cells.
2 — Pseudohypha: joined elongated cells with constrictions at the junctions.
What it looks like: Budding oval yeasts and segmented pseudohyphae; hyphae "skewer" epithelial cells.
Key feature: Segmented threads + budding yeasts.
What it means: Consistent with vulvovaginal candidiasis; asymptomatic colonisation is possible — judge with the clinical picture.
Stain / preparation: KOH / Gram / Pap
Caveat: Not every Candida species forms pseudohyphae; interpret with symptoms and tests.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Inflammation (many neutrophils)
slides.caption:
1 — Neutrophils with multilobed nuclei.
2 — A large epithelial cell for comparison.
What it looks like: Many segmented neutrophils among and over epithelial cells.
Key feature: More leukocytes than epithelial cells.
What it means: A sign of inflammation (e.g. trichomoniasis, cervicitis). Heavy inflammation can obscure epithelium and limit assessment.
Stain / preparation: Pap or another stained smear
Caveat: Many neutrophils signal inflammation but not its cause.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Gonococci (Gram stain)
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — Neutrophil with a multilobed nucleus.
2 — Pink-red, paired, bean-shaped cocci in the cytoplasm (drawn enlarged).
What it looks like: Paired, bean-shaped, red-pink (Gram-negative) diplococci with facing concave sides — inside neutrophils.
Key feature: Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci.
What it means: Highly reliable for gonorrhoea in male urethral smears. Low sensitivity in cervical smears — NAAT is recommended.
Stain / preparation: Gram
Caveat: A negative endocervical Gram smear does not exclude gonorrhoea — NAAT may be needed.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Koilocyte
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — A sharply bordered, irregular perinuclear cavity (halo).
2 — Enlarged dark nucleus with an irregular outline; dense cytoplasm at the rim.
What it looks like: A large clear perinuclear cavity with a sharp edge (halo) and a dense cytoplasmic rim. Enlarged, dark, irregular ("raisinoid") nucleus, often binucleate.
Key feature: Halo + abnormal nucleus. A plain nucleus means it is not one.
What it means: A sign of HPV effect; reported as LSIL in Bethesda.
Confused with: Small perinuclear clearing (glycogen, inflammation) — vague edge and a normal nucleus.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: A halo alone is not enough: nuclear atypia must be present.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: HSIL: high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, scant cytoplasm.
2 — Irregular nuclear outline, coarse dark chromatin.
What it looks like: Small immature cells, often in groups. The nucleus fills most of the cell; dark, irregular, coarse chromatin.
Key feature: High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Compare with an intermediate nucleus.
What it means: High likelihood of a precancerous lesion. The clinician decides next steps per ASCCP 2019 — colposcopy or expedited treatment. The cytologist reports.
Confused with: Parabasal and metaplastic cells — smooth nuclei, fine chromatin.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: The drawing explains HSIL features; a cytologist makes the final call.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: The Bethesda System (2014)
rows: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy
Normal. Organisms and reactive changes are reported separately.
Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance
The commonest equivocal result; usually triaged with an HPV test.
Usually HPV effect (koilocytes); often regresses. The clinician decides next steps.
Atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL
A high-grade lesion is possible — colposcopy is usual.
High likelihood of precancer. The clinician decides next steps per ASCCP 2019 — colposcopy or expedited treatment (without prior biopsy).

slides.title: The Bethesda System (2014)
rows: Atypical glandular cells (endocervical, endometrial or not otherwise specified — NOS)

Glandular abnormality; the clinician decides the work-up (ASCCP 2019, non-pregnant patients: colposcopy with endocervical sampling; at age 35 or older, and under 35 at increased risk of endometrial neoplasia — e.g. abnormal uterine bleeding, signs of chronic anovulation or obesity — endometrial sampling as well; for atypical endometrial cells, endometrial and endocervical sampling first).
Atypical glandular cells, favor neoplastic (endocervical or not otherwise specified)
Falls short of AIS or adenocarcinoma, but neoplasia is likely. The clinician decides the work-up per ASCCP 2019.
Adenocarcinoma (endocervical, endometrial, extrauterine or not otherwise specified — NOS)
Malignant glandular cells — urgent specialist referral.

slides.title: Taking and staining the cytology smear
bullets: Patient preparation: Outside menstruation. Avoid intercourse, douching, vaginal medicines and spermicides for 2 days before.
Sampling: Spatula from the ectocervix and brush from the endocervical canal, covering the transformation zone.
Smear and fixation: Thin, even layer. For Pap — immediate wet fixation (95% alcohol or spray); air-drying distorts nuclei. For liquid-based cytology rinse the device into the vial.
Staining: Pap: nuclei — haematoxylin (blue); cytoplasm — OG-6 and EA (pink or blue-green). Romanowsky — air-dried smear. Gram — for bacterial vaginosis (Nugent) and gonococci.
Common errors: Thick smear; delayed fixation (drying artefact); blood or heavy inflammation obscuring cells; scant cellularity; no endocervical cells (transformation zone not sampled).

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: from age 30 a high-performance (HPV) test every 5–10 years; in people living with HIV from age 25 every 3–5 years years
≥3 of 4: homogeneous thin discharge, "clue" cells, vaginal pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH —

slides.title: Pap result: ASC-US. Per NCI, what is the usual next step?
options: Do nothing and repeat in 10 years
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: ASC-US is the most common abnormal finding; an HPV test shows whether HPV is the cause.

slides.title: A Pap smear has too few cells, hidden by mucus. What is this result called?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: NCI: unsatisfactory — too few cells, or cells hidden by blood or mucus; repeat in 2–4 months.

slides.title: What is needed to diagnose BV by the Amsel criteria?
options: At least three of the four criteria
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: At least three of four: homogeneous thin discharge, clue cells, pH > 4.5, fishy odour with KOH.

slides.title: A vaginal wet mount was read 2 hours after collection; no trichomonads were seen. Conclusion?
options: A KOH mount shows trichomonads better
Unreliable; confirm with a molecular test (NAAT)
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The slide should have been read immediately.

Basis: CDC: sensitivity drops to 20% within an hour; NAAT is advised after a negative wet mount.

options: separately from the vaginal portion of the cervix and separately from the cervical canal

Advantages and disadvantages of vaginal smear staining methods (Romanowsky, Papanicolaou, Gram and methylene blue staining)?
bullets: 1. Papanicolaou staining (wet fixation, hematoxylin + OG-6 + EA): shows nuclear structure clearly, the cytoplasm is transparent (seeing through layers), distinguishes keratinization and degree of maturation – the standard for cervical screening and tumor cytology; disadvantage – multi-step, requires time and reagents.

2. Romanowsky-type stains (air-dried): quick, simple, show cytoplasm and granules, microorganisms and blood cells well; disadvantage – nuclear detail and keratinization are poorer, cells enlarge on air-drying.

3. Gram staining: microflora (lactobacilli – gram-positive rods, Gardnerella/anaerobes, "clue" cells, gonococci – gram-negative diplococci) – the Nugent score for bacterial vaginosis (the reference laboratory method); disadvantage – not for cell morphology.

slides.title: Advantages and disadvantages of vaginal smear staining methods (Romanowsky, Papanicolaou, Gram and methylene blue staining)?
bullets: 4. Simple methylene blue staining: quick, cheap – shows leukocytes, "clue" cells, diplococci tentatively; low specificity, gives no Gram characteristics.
5. Chosen according to the purpose: tumor screening – Papanicolaou; microflora/STI – Gram (and wet mount, NAAT if needed).

slides.title: Preparing a PAP smear: requirements for the patient and for taking the smear, as well as for staining?
bullets: 1. Requirements for the patient: days outside menstruation are preferred (in liquid-based cytology menstruation interferes little), avoid intercourse, douching, vaginal medications, spermicides for 48 hours beforehand; with acute inflammation, treat first.

2. Taking the smear: speculum (if needed moistened with water only), the cervix clearly visible; from the transformation zone and endocervix with a special brush (cervex-brush, cytobrush) or spatula; visible suspicious areas.
3. Slide: conventional – spread evenly thin on the slide and fix wet immediately (avoid drying artifact); liquid-based – rinse the brush in a vial with preservative.
4. Staining: Papanicolaou (hematoxylin – nucleus; OG-6 and EA – cytoplasm), reagent quality checked with control slides.

slides.title: Preparing a PAP smear: requirements for the patient and for taking the smear, as well as for staining?
bullets: 5. Adequacy criteria: sufficient squamous cellularity, transformation zone component (endocervical/metaplastic cells), not obscured by blood, inflammation or drying; otherwise recorded as "unsatisfactory".

slides.title: Cytological examination of smears from the vaginal portion of the cervix by the Bethesda 2001 system: smears within normal limits and reactive changes?
bullets: 1. The current system is Bethesda 2014 (an update of the 2001 edition): specimen adequacy, general category and descriptive interpretation.
2. NILM (negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy): normal superficial, intermediate, parabasal cells; endocervical cells and transformation zone component.
3. Organisms falling under NILM: Trichomonas vaginalis, Candida, flora change suggesting bacterial vaginosis ("clue" cells), Actinomyces, herpes virus effect.

4. Reactive changes (NILM): inflammation (including repair), radiation effect, changes associated with an intrauterine device; atrophy (postmenopause – predominance of parabasal cells); predominance of intermediate cells under progesterone.
5. Distinguishing reactive changes from ASC-US and other lesions: nuclear enlargement is uniform, chromatin fine, nucleoli may be present, N/C ratio preserved.
